title: Fra Angelico (d. 1455)
hookLine: a Dominican friar who painted the Annunciation on his brothers' cell walls

cards: Before dawn, in a convent in Florence, a friar wakes in a small bare cell: a bed, a window, a desk. Before he sees anything else, he sees a scene from the Gospel on his wall.
Not hung there; painted right into the plaster. Down the corridor, cell after cell has its own. The painter was a friar of that same house, a brother who walked the same corridor.

teach.b: Start with who he was. Fra Angelico was a Dominican friar, a brother of the Order of Preachers, and a painter. Fra means brother.
Angelico, angelic, is the name people gave him, for his work and for his life.

teach.h: THE GOSPEL ON THE CELL WALLS.
teach.b: Next, the walls. At the convent of San Marco in Florence, he painted scenes from the life of Christ in his brothers' cells. They weren't there for visitors.
They were for the friar who lived with them, to pray with: few figures, plain backgrounds, a great deal of quiet. Then, the Annunciation.
At the top of the stairs to the cells, he painted the moment in Luke's Gospel when the angel Gabriel comes to Mary.
In the Douay-Rheims, the angel says, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." And Mary answers, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."

In the painting, the angel leans in, Mary leans toward him with her arms folded across her chest, and nothing else in the scene moves. Some viewers read it as the moment before her yes. Finally, why it counts as prayer.
Giorgio Vasari, who wrote lives of the Italian artists after him, says Fra Angelico prayed before he took up his brush.
The Church later beatified him and named him a patron of artists. A Dominican's work is to preach. He preached without a sermon, on a wall, to one brother at a time.

how: Catholics pray with images in churches and homes, and the Angelus, prayed by some at morning, noon and evening, recalls the Annunciation with the angel's greeting and Mary's answer.

games.why: he painted quiet scenes from the life of Christ, few figures and plain backgrounds, for each brother to pray with.

practice: Find one Annunciation, Fra Angelico's from San Marco if you can, or any other, on a screen, a card, a church window, or in memory, and look for a minute without analyzing: where does the light fall, which way is each one leaning?
Then close your eyes and keep the picture. If you pray, pray the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; if not, rest in the quiet of the picture.
